doc.title: Tim Ries interviewed by Monk Rowe, Utica, New York, March 19, 2022

title: Where ideas come from; striving for Coltrane's level while accepting today
summary: Asked about technique and ideas, Ries describes community in a small club and reaching for the standard of Coltrane, Parker and Young while allowing music to come through.

story.theme_name: Teaching jazz: schools, students and advice to the young
story.community_name: What to think while improvising: wrong notes and being in the moment

blocks.x: I’m not sure how to ask this but after hearing you play, which was really terrific last night, I should tell our viewers it was in Utica, New York at a cool little place called The Other Side. It seems to me you have abundant technique to play whatever you want. I’m going to go from that premise. So is the challenge not so much how to play it but what to think of? What is something tonight that I can do that I haven’t done repeatedly, and if that statement is sort of true, where do your ideas come from?

Well thank you for the kind words. It was a really cool place to play actually, The Other Side, and it was a nice gallery with art work and stuff. And then it was filled with people but with 60 — it was like packed but it’s a small place. But really, talking to people before, during the break and then afterwards really, it’s a kind of a cool thing about jazz or this improvised music is that those people were there to really hear music and they stayed, and then talking to them and just you realize that this music is really about community in a sense not only on the stage but then a small audience you get that more than you can in a big arena or a big theater, where you can really engage with the people, like local people. And get to know them. And that feeling is really cool. But as far as the technique and what to play while improvising, and what not to do — you know it’s almost what not to do in a sense. But the idea like do you know as an individual, a person, whatever instrument that you’re playing there’s all the years that it takes to get to the place where you can be able to facilitate with the ideas that you have. So the more technique you have, like someone like John Coltrane or Freddie Hubbard or you know, Art Tatum or somebody with just the most incredible technique and you hear that and you just realize that the true brilliant maestros of the music from the past and there are so many, you know it’s almost like okay that’s there and I’m probably never going to reach that level. I’m trying. I’m trying to reach the level of Coltrane and Charlie Parker and Lester Young. That’s been set, that standard of brilliance. So I’m trying to attain that in my practicing and trying to develop a technique so that I can get there. You know so I’m trying to reach the mountaintop. And it took me a long time to realize okay that’s there and I’m going to try to get there but I’m going to be satisfied with what I’m doing today, so not judging myself as I’m playing, which is really hard. So as you are that day kind of playing whatever happens. And I truly believe that music — and maybe it’s ‘cause of my father and seeing that vibe is like I think that the music is there. It’s already in the atmosphere or it’s coming from a high spiritual place, that if you are accepting of that, if you just allow it to come through you and don’t get in the way of it, not to diminish the technique. So you need technique to be able to like play that note in tune, so you need the technique for just the rudimentary aspect of the instrument. But then that’s just technique.

Then you have to just allow the music to happen. And that’s what’s the beautiful part about improvised music and jazz is that then you also hear the drummer do something or Ron last night playing the organ, okay the way he chorded it, or like that connection you have, the conversation. So then it’s a combination of like accepting what’s coming in, accepting what’s happening around you, and then the feeling of the room, actually when you kind of just sense the vibes from the people. There’s all that combination it plays a part of it. And you know I think last night was just really special because you know playing with good musicians in a cool place with good people there, it all adds, that all comes together.
